title: Inertia: why moving things keep moving and still things stay still

summary.text: Walk across a room and drop a pair of rolled socks over a plate. They land past the plate, not on it. The socks were moving forward with you, and they kept moving forward as they fell. Every thing keeps doing what it is doing, staying still or moving in a straight line at the same speed, until a force changes it. Scientists call this inertia, and Isaac Newton made it his first law of motion in 1687. On Earth, friction and the air slowly stop moving things, so a ball on a rough floor soon stops. On smooth ice it slides much further, and in empty space, with nothing to slow it, it would never stop. That is why you need a seatbelt, why a coin can drop into a tumbler when a card is flicked away, and why you never feel the Earth carrying you round at great speed.
summary.art: A child walking across a tiled room in Chennai, letting go of a rolled pair of socks above a steel plate on the floor. A dotted curved line shows the socks falling forward and landing past the plate. In a small corner picture, a ball slides across shiny ice.

intro.hook: Try this. Put a card on top of a steel tumbler and a coin on the card. Pull the card away slowly. Now set it up again and flick the card away hard and fast with your finger. Where did the coin go each time? Nothing pushed the coin down into the tumbler. So why did it end up inside?
intro.text: The coin was sitting still, and it went on sitting still while the card shot out from under it. Then gravity pulled it straight down into the tumbler. This is inertia: things keep doing what they are already doing until a force changes it. In this unit you test it with your own body, with socks, eggs, water and marbles. You find out why a rolling ball on Earth always stops, why a ball on ice slides so far, and why a spacecraft launched in 1977 is still travelling today.
intro.art: A steel tumbler with a square of card on top and a five-rupee coin on the card. A finger flicks the card sideways, the card flies off, and the coin drops straight into the tumbler.

outcomes: I can say Newton's first law in my own words: a thing keeps still, or keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, until a force changes it.
I can use the word inertia, and explain the coin and card trick and the walking drop with it.
I can run a fair test of where a dropped thing lands when I walk at different speeds, record it in a table, and explain the results.
I can explain why a rolling ball stops on a rough floor but slides much further on ice, using the words friction and air resistance.
I can explain why passengers need seatbelts and why water slops in a tumbler when a bus brakes.
I can explain why we do not feel the Earth moving, and tell how Aryabhata and Pierre Gassendi thought about moving boats and ships.
I can say what scientists still do not know about why things have inertia at all.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. A force can start a thing moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down or turn it.
terms.example: Your kick is a force that starts a football moving.
terms.art: A foot kicking a football, with an arrow showing the push.

terms.meaning: Moving from one place to another. A thing in motion is moving.
terms.example: An auto driving down the road is in motion.
terms.art: An auto-rickshaw on a road with three faint copies behind it showing where it has been.

terms.meaning: Not moving at all, compared with the things around it.
terms.example: A tumbler standing on the table is at rest.
terms.art: A steel tumbler standing still on a wooden table.

terms.meaning: The way every thing keeps doing what it is doing. A still thing stays still, and a moving thing keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line, until a force changes it.
terms.example: When a bus brakes suddenly, the passengers lurch forward, because their bodies keep moving.
terms.art: Passengers in a city bus leaning forward as the bus brakes, holding the bars.

terms.meaning: Isaac Newton's rule, from 1687: a thing stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless a force acts on it.
terms.example: A puck on an air hockey table glides a long way after one tap, because almost nothing slows it.
terms.art: A hand tapping a puck on an air hockey table, with a long straight arrow ahead of the puck.

terms.meaning: A short rule that says what always happens, tested many times by many people. A law says what happens, not always why.
terms.example: Newton's first law says what moving things do. It does not say why they do it.
terms.art: An open notebook with one rule written in it and many ticks beside it.

terms.meaning: The grip between two surfaces that touch. It works against sliding and rolling, and slows moving things down.
terms.example: A marble rolling on a towel stops quickly, because the towel gives a lot of friction.
terms.art: A marble rolling slowly to a stop on a bath towel.

terms.meaning: The push of the air on a thing moving through it. It slows the thing down.
terms.example: A flat sheet of paper drifts down slowly, because air resistance pushes up on it.
terms.art: A sheet of paper drifting down, with small arrows of air pushing up under it.

terms.meaning: How much matter a thing has. More mass means more inertia: the thing is harder to start, stop or turn.
terms.example: A full gas cylinder is much harder to push into motion than an empty one.
terms.art: A child pushing an empty water can easily and struggling with a full one.

terms.meaning: How far a thing moves in a certain time.
terms.example: A cycle at 10 kilometres an hour goes 10 kilometres in one hour.
terms.art: A girl on a cycle passing a road sign with distance marks.

terms.meaning: The way a thing is moving, such as forward, left or up.
terms.example: A cricket ball hit straight changes direction when a fielder's hands stop it.
terms.art: A cricket ball with an arrow, flying towards a fielder's cupped hands.

terms.meaning: A strong strap that holds a passenger in the seat. It gives the force that stops the passenger when the car stops suddenly.
terms.example: Everyone in a car, front and back, should wear a seatbelt.
terms.art: A girl in the back seat of a car with her seatbelt across her shoulder and lap.

explanations.concept: Inertia: things keep doing what they are doing
explanations.definition: Every thing keeps doing what it is already doing. If it is still, it stays still. If it is moving, it keeps moving at the same speed in the same straight line. Only a force can change this. This is called inertia.
explanations.description: Isaac Newton wrote this down in 1687 as his first law of motion. It sounds simple, but it surprises most people. We see moving things stop all the time, so we think stopping happens by itself. It does not. Something always stops them: friction, the air, a wall or a hand. In the walking drop, the socks kept moving forward after you let go, because nothing pushed them back. They landed past the plate.
examples: A coin on a card stays still when the card is flicked away fast, and drops into the tumbler.
Rolled socks dropped while you walk land ahead of where you let go.
When an auto brakes, the passengers lurch forward.
explanations.art: Three small pictures in a row: a coin dropping into a tumbler, socks landing past a plate, and passengers leaning forward in a braking auto.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the unit, inertia. It is Isaac Newton's first law of motion.

explanations.definition: A thing at rest stays at rest until a force moves it. A force also needs time to get it moving.
explanations.description: When you pull the card slowly, friction between the card and the coin acts for a long time, and the coin moves with the card. When you flick the card fast, friction acts for only a tiny moment. That is far too short to get the coin moving. So the coin stays where it was, with nothing under it, and gravity pulls it down into the tumbler. A heavier coin, with more mass, stays behind even better. The same idea explains the carrom tower: hit the bottom coin hard and fast, and only that coin shoots out.
examples: Flick the card, and the coin drops into the tumbler.
Strike the bottom coin of a tower of carrom coins, and the rest drop straight down.
Pull a newspaper fast from under a plastic tumbler, and the tumbler hardly moves.
explanations.art: A tower of carrom coins on a carrom board. A striker has just knocked out the bottom coin, which is sliding away, while the rest of the tower drops straight down.
explanations.context: This card is about still things, such as the coin in the card trick. It says why they stay still.

explanations.definition: A moving thing keeps moving at the same speed, in a straight line, until a force speeds it up, slows it down or turns it.
explanations.description: Nothing has to keep pushing a moving thing to keep it going. A push is needed only to change its motion. The Voyager 1 spacecraft was launched in 1977. Its rockets stopped firing long ago, yet it is still moving away from the Sun at about 17 kilometres every second. There is almost nothing in space to slow it down. Inside a raw egg, the runny inside keeps turning after you stop the shell, and it sets the shell turning again.
examples: Voyager 1 is still travelling out of the solar system, almost 50 years after launch, with no engine pushing it forward.
A raw egg starts spinning again after you stop it for a moment.
Water stirred in a steel bowl keeps turning after you take the spoon out.
explanations.art: The Voyager spacecraft, with its big white dish, moving through dark space far from a tiny Sun, with a long dotted line behind it.
explanations.context: This card is about moving things. It says what keeps them moving.

explanations.concept: Why things on Earth stop: friction and air resistance
explanations.definition: On Earth, moving things slow down and stop because forces act on them: friction from the surface they touch, and air resistance from the air.
explanations.description: Roll a marble from the same ramp onto a towel, a doormat and a bare floor. On the towel it stops after a short way, because the towel gives a lot of friction. On the smooth floor it rolls much further. Ice is smoother and more slippery still, so a ball or a stone slides a very long way on ice. The less friction and air resistance, the further a thing goes. With none at all, it would never stop. This is the 'ball on ice' that the first law is often explained with.
examples: A marble stops quickly on a towel but rolls across a tiled floor.
A stone slid across a frozen lake glides a long way.
An air hockey puck floats on a thin layer of air, so it glides far after one tap.
explanations.art: Three strips side by side: a towel, a doormat and shiny floor tiles, each with a marble and a line showing how far it rolled. The line on the tiles is longest. Beside them, a strip of ice with an even longer line.
explanations.context: This card answers a puzzle: if moving things keep moving, why does a rolling ball always stop?

explanations.definition: A moving thing goes in a straight line unless a force turns it. Changing direction is a change of motion, so it needs a force.
explanations.description: Swing a rolled sock on a string in a circle, and the string pulls the sock towards your hand all the time. That pull keeps turning it. Let go of the string, and the sock flies off in a straight line, the way it was going at that moment. It does not keep curving. When a bus turns left, your body keeps going straight, so you lean against the side of the bus. The bus turns, and you are carried round only when the seat or the bar pushes on you.
examples: When a bus turns a corner, passengers lean towards the outside of the turn.
A sock swung on a string flies off in a straight line when you let go.
Water flies off a wet umbrella in straight lines when you spin it.
explanations.art: A view from above of a girl swinging a sock on a string in a circle. A dotted straight line shows where the sock flies when she lets go, along the edge of the circle.
explanations.context: This card is about changing direction. It says why a thing swung in a circle flies off straight when you let go.

explanations.definition: The more mass a thing has, the more inertia it has. It needs a bigger force to start it, stop it or turn it.
explanations.description: A loaded lorry needs a much longer distance to stop than a cycle going at the same speed. Its brakes must take away the motion of all that mass. A heavy coin or a stack of coins stays behind better in the card trick than a light one. In the raw egg, the runny inside has mass, so it keeps turning when the shell stops. Mass is the amount of matter in a thing, and inertia grows with it.
examples: An empty steel almirah is easier to push into motion than a full one.
A loaded lorry needs a longer road to stop than a car.
Two stacked ten-rupee coins drop into the tumbler more surely than one small light coin.
explanations.art: A cycle and a loaded lorry braking on the same road, the lorry with a much longer brake mark behind it.
explanations.context: This card is about heavy things and light things. It says why heavy things are harder to start and stop.

explanations.concept: A smoothly moving room feels still
explanations.definition: Inside a train, a ship or a lift that moves smoothly in a straight line at a steady speed, everything behaves just as it does at rest. A ball tossed straight up falls back into your hand.
explanations.description: The ball is moving forward with the train before you toss it. While it is in the air, it keeps that forward motion, so it keeps up with you and your hand. You can feel the train only when it speeds up, slows down or turns. The Earth carries you too. In Chennai, the spinning Earth carries you east at about 1,600 kilometres an hour, and the Earth carries all of us round the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second. You do not feel either, because the motion is smooth and everything around you moves with you. Around 499 CE, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote that the stars seem to move west only because the Earth turns. He compared it to a person in a moving boat, who sees the trees on the bank moving backwards.
examples: In a smoothly moving train, a ball tossed straight up lands back in your hand.
In a lift moving at a steady speed, you feel nothing. You feel a push only when it starts and stops.
You cannot feel the Earth spin, though everywhere in India it carries you east at more than 1,300 kilometres an hour.
explanations.art: A girl sitting in a train compartment tossing a small ball straight up and catching it, while fields and palm trees blur past the window.
explanations.context: This card explains why you feel nothing in a smooth train, and why you cannot feel the Earth moving.

explanations.definition: When a car, bus or auto stops suddenly, the passengers keep moving forward at the old speed until a force stops them. A seatbelt gives that force safely.
explanations.description: Put a small atta-dough person on a toy car and roll it into a book. The car stops at the book, but the dough person keeps going and flies off the front. With a rubber band across the dough person, they stay on. A real seatbelt works the same way. It holds you to the seat, so you stop with the car, gently, instead of hitting the seat in front or the windscreen. A two-wheeler rider has no seatbelt, so a helmet protects the head if they are thrown off.
examples: A dough person flies off a toy car that hits a book, unless they are tied on.
A school bag on the back seat slides forward when the car brakes hard.
Water in a tumbler slops forward when a bus brakes.
explanations.art: A toy car stopped against a book, with an atta-dough person flying forward off it. Next to it, the same car with the dough person held on by a rubber band.
explanations.context: This card uses inertia to explain why everyone in a car should wear a seatbelt.

explanations.definition: Newton wrote three laws of motion in his book Principia in 1687. The first is inertia. The second says a bigger force changes motion more, and more mass needs more force. The third says forces come in pairs: when you push something, it pushes back on you just as hard.
explanations.description: This unit is mostly about the first law, because the other two build on it. You can feel the second law when you push an empty trolley and a full one with the same push: the empty one speeds up much more. You can feel the third law when you push a wall: the wall pushes you back. Newton built on the work of many others, including Galileo Galilei in Italy and Pierre Gassendi and René Descartes in France.
examples: First law: a coin stays still when a card is flicked from under it.
Second law: the same push speeds up an empty trolley more than a full one.
Third law: a balloon pushes air out of the back, and the air pushes the balloon forward.
explanations.art: Three small panels: a coin above a tumbler, a child pushing a trolley, and a balloon rocket on a string.
explanations.context: This card names all three of Newton's laws of motion, so you know where inertia fits.

explanations.concept: Why do things have inertia at all?
explanations.description: Newton's law says what things do, but not why. Nobody knows for sure why mass resists being started, stopped or turned. Scientists have measured inertia very exactly for hundreds of years, and the law has passed every test on Earth and in space. But the reason underneath is still argued about.
examples: Mass and inertia always go together: a thing with twice the mass has twice the inertia.
Spacecraft are steered using Newton's laws, and they arrive where expected.

perspectives.explanation: Newton thought there is one fixed, unmoving space, and inertia is how matter resists changing its motion through that space.

perspectives.who: Ernst Mach, an Austrian scientist, in the 1880s
perspectives.explanation: Mach suggested that a thing's inertia might come from all the other matter in the universe, the far-away stars and galaxies. Nobody has shown whether this is true.

Most of the mass of the things around you comes from the energy holding the tiny parts inside atoms together. So inertia may be a property of energy itself. This explains where mass comes from, but the deepest why is still open.

explanations.art: A child looking up at a night sky full of stars and galaxies, holding a ball in one hand, with a question mark drawn faintly between the ball and the stars.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: why things have inertia at all.

agreed.text: A thing stays at rest, or keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line, unless a force acts on it. This is Newton's first law.
agreed.evidence: It has been tested for over 300 years, on Earth and in space. Spacecraft such as Voyager 1 travel exactly as the law predicts.

agreed.text: Moving things on Earth stop because of forces such as friction and air resistance, not by themselves.
agreed.evidence: The smoother the surface, the further a ball rolls from the same ramp. On ice, or on an air hockey table, things glide much further.

agreed.text: The more mass a thing has, the more force is needed to change its motion.
agreed.evidence: Pushing an empty and a full trolley shows it. Lorries need longer to stop than cars at the same speed.

agreed.text: Inside a room that moves smoothly at a steady speed, nothing inside behaves differently from a room at rest.
agreed.evidence: Gassendi's stone, dropped from the mast of a moving ship in 1640, landed at the foot of the mast. A ball tossed up in a smooth train lands back in your hand.

challenging.claim: A moving thing needs a push all the time to keep moving.
challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,300 years ago, and the everyday feeling of most people
challenging.for: Stop pedalling a cycle and it slows down. Stop pushing a trolley and it stops.
challenging.against: The cycle and the trolley are slowed by friction and air resistance. Take those away, as on ice or in space, and moving things keep going.
challenging.context: This card is about the oldest wrong idea about motion.

challenging.claim: When you drop something while walking, it falls straight down to the spot where you let go.
challenging.who: A very common guess, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: To the person who drops it, it seems to fall straight down beside their legs.
challenging.against: In the walking drop, the socks land past the target, because they keep their forward motion while they fall. Seen from the side, they fall in a curve.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many people make in the walking drop.

challenging.claim: If the Earth were really moving, a stone dropped from a tall tower would land far behind it.
challenging.who: People who argued against a moving Earth, in Europe before about 1640
challenging.for: It seems the ground should move away under a falling stone.
challenging.against: The stone is moving with the Earth before it is dropped, and it keeps that motion. Gassendi showed the same on a moving ship.
challenging.context: This card is about an old argument that the Earth cannot be moving.

challenging.claim: Inertia comes from all the other matter in the universe.
challenging.who: Ernst Mach, in the 1880s, and some physicists since
challenging.for: It is hard to say what 'moving' means except compared with other things, such as the far-away stars.
challenging.against: Nobody has found a test that shows this. Most physicists treat it as an interesting idea, not a settled one.
challenging.context: This card is about an open idea: where inertia comes from.

challenging.claim: Heavy things keep moving because they are heavy, and light things stop because they are light.
challenging.for: A light paper ball thrown hard soon stops, while a cricket ball goes far.
challenging.against: The paper ball is slowed more by air resistance, because it is light for its size. In a place with no air, both would keep moving. Mass makes things harder to stop, but light things have inertia too.
challenging.context: This card is about a mix-up between inertia and air resistance.

big_questions.q: In the walking drop, you saw the socks fall straight down beside you, but your helper saw them fall in a curve. Who saw what really happened?
big_questions.hint: Both of you watched carefully. Could the path of a falling thing depend on who is watching, and how that person is moving?

big_questions.q: You are sitting still on a sofa, yet the Earth carries you round the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second. Are you still or moving?
big_questions.hint: Still compared with what? The sofa? The Sun? The stars?

big_questions.q: If nothing ever slowed it down, would a rolling marble roll for ever?
big_questions.hint: Think about the towel, the floor and the ice. What happens as the slowing force gets smaller and smaller?

big_questions.q: Newton's law says what things do, but not why. Is it enough to know what always happens, or do we need to know why?
big_questions.hint: People sent spacecraft to Saturn using the law, without knowing the deepest why.

big_questions.q: Your body has inertia too. Is it harder for you to start something new, or to stop something you are already doing?
big_questions.hint: Think of getting out of bed, or stopping a game when it is time to eat.

big_questions.q: Voyager 1 will keep moving for millions of years. Can anything really keep going for ever?
big_questions.hint: Space is almost empty, but not quite. And what about the Earth going round the Sun?

story.title: The Ball on the Madurai Train
story.note: Kavya, Arun, their grandfather and this journey are made up. Trains really run between Chennai and Madurai through Tiruchirappalli. Aryabhata's boat comparison is real: it is in his book, the Aryabhatiya, written around 499 CE.
text: The train left Chennai Egmore at six in the morning, while the sky was still pink. Kavya had the window seat. She was nine. Her little brother Arun, who was six, sat in the middle, and Thatha, their grandfather, sat by the aisle with a steel flask of coffee on his knees. They were going to Madurai for their cousin's wedding.
By seven o'clock the train was going very fast. Coconut palms, paddy fields and a white temple tower slid past the window. Arun had a small red rubber ball. He held it tight in both hands.
'Throw it to me,' said Kavya.
Arun shook his head. 'If I throw it up, the train will go on without it. It will fly to the back of the train. It might go out of the door.'
Thatha nodded slowly. 'He may be right, Kavya. This train is going faster than a car on the highway. A ball in the air has nothing holding it. The train will move away under it.'

Kavya thought about this. It did sound sensible. Then she remembered last week, at home in the hall. She had walked past a steel plate on the floor and dropped a pair of rolled socks right above it. Everyone had guessed the socks would land on the plate. They had landed past it, every time. The faster she walked, the further past they went.
'I don't think it will fly to the back,' she said. 'I think it will land right back in Arun's hand.'
'Why?' asked Thatha.
'Because the ball is already going as fast as the train,' said Kavya. 'It's going as fast as us. When Arun throws it up, nothing pushes it backwards. So it keeps going forward, with us.'
Thatha raised his eyebrows. 'Hmm. Let's test it, then. But only a little way up, Arun. Not to the fan.'
Arun's hands were shaking a bit. He tossed the ball up, just above his head. It went up. It came down. It landed, plop, in his open hands.
He stared at it. 'It stayed with me!'
'Do it again,' said Kavya. He did it ten times. Every time, the ball came straight back down into his hands, as if the train were standing still in a station.
Thatha was quiet for a while. Then he laughed. 'Seventy years I have been riding trains,' he said, 'and I never once tried that.'

Near Tiruchirappalli, Thatha poured coffee from his flask into a paper cup. Just then the train began to brake for the station. Arun was holding the ball up again, ready to toss it. He let go just as the brakes squealed. This time the ball did not land in his hands. It landed on Kavya's knee, a little in front of him. And Thatha's coffee slopped over the front edge of the paper cup, onto his white veshti.
'Aiyo!' said Thatha, dabbing at it with his towel.
'Look,' said Kavya. 'The coffee went forward, and so did the ball. The train slowed down, but the coffee didn't. It kept going at the old speed, so it slopped forward. The ball too.'
'So the ball only stays with us,' said Arun slowly, 'when the train goes smooth?'

'Yes,' said Kavya. 'When the train goes smooth and straight, everything inside goes with it, and you can't even feel that you're moving. You only feel it when the train speeds up, slows down or turns.'

Arun closed his eyes. 'I can't feel anything now,' he said, because the train had pulled away from the station and was running smoothly again. 'If I didn't look out of the window, I wouldn't know we were moving.'

Kavya looked out of the window at the fields sliding backwards. 'Thatha, did you know that Aryabhata wrote about this, about fifteen hundred years ago?' she said. 'Amma read it to me. He said that when you sit in a moving boat, the trees on the bank seem to move backwards. And he said the stars seem to move across the sky for the same reason. They're not really moving round us. The Earth is turning, and we're turning with it.'
'So we're moving now,' said Arun, 'even when the train is stopped?'
'All the time,' said Kavya. 'Even when you're asleep. The Earth carries us round, smooth as anything, so we never feel it.'
Arun held the ball very still in his lap, as if it might fly away. Then he grinned, and tossed it up again.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the ball was moving forward at the train's speed before Arun tossed it. Once in the air, nothing pushed it backwards, so it kept that forward speed, and stayed above his hands. This is inertia, Newton's first law. When the train braked, the train and Arun's hands slowed down, but the ball and the coffee kept their speed for a moment, so they moved forward. Inside anything moving smoothly in a straight line at a steady speed, everything behaves as if it were still. That is why we cannot feel the Earth turning, which Aryabhata understood around 499 CE.
ask: Why did Arun think the ball would fly to the back of the train?
What had Kavya seen at home that made her think differently?
Why did the coffee slop forward when the train braked?
Thatha had ridden trains for seventy years but never tested the ball. Why do you think people often don't test the things they are sure about?
If you can't feel the Earth moving, how do you think people found out that it does?

The boy tossing the red ball a little way up, everyone watching, the fields blurred outside the window.
The ball landing in the boy's cupped hands, the boy's mouth open in surprise.
The grandfather's coffee slopping forward out of a paper cup as the train brakes, the ball landing on the girl's knee.

games.title: Keep Going or Change?
games.context: This is a card game about Newton's first law. Each card shows a moment. You say whether a force acts, and what happens next.

printables.title: 20 moment cards to cut out
items: A football rolls across the grass. (Change: friction from the grass slows it down.)
A coin sits on a table. Nobody touches it. (Keep going: it stays still.)
An auto brakes suddenly. What do the passengers do? (Keep going: they lurch forward.)
A spacecraft far out in space has its engines off. (Keep going: it moves on at the same speed.)
A bus turns left. What does a standing passenger do? (Keep going: they lean to the right, the outside of the turn.)
A marble rolls onto a towel. (Change: friction stops it quickly.)
A stone slides across a frozen lake. (Keep going for a long way: ice gives very little friction.)
A girl walking lets go of a ball. Where does it land? (Keep going: ahead of where she let go.)
A puck glides on an air hockey table. (Keep going, almost: very little slows it.)
A card is flicked from under a coin on a tumbler. (Keep going: the coin stays still, then falls in.)
A cricket ball is caught by a fielder. (Change: the fielder's hands stop it.)
A swing goes back and forth. (Change: gravity keeps changing its motion.)
A football lies still, and then you kick it. (Change: the kick starts it moving.)
Water is stirred in a bowl and the spoon is taken out. (Keep going: the water turns for a while.)
A sock swung on a string is let go. (Keep going: straight, not round.)
You toss a ball up in a smooth train. (Keep going: it moves forward with you and lands in your hand.)
A loaded lorry and a cycle brake together. Which needs longer to stop? (The lorry: more mass, more inertia.)
A raw egg is stopped and let go. (Keep going: the inside keeps turning.)
A rolling marble with no friction and no air at all. (Keep going: for ever.)
You stand still on the Earth. Are you moving? (Yes: the Earth carries you round.)

setup.caption: 1. Cut out the moment cards and shuffle them.

setup.caption: 2. Hear a card. Say 'keep going' or 'change', and name the force.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
On your turn, another player reads you a card, without the answer in the brackets. Playing alone? Read it yourself and cover the answer.
Say 'keep going' if no force changes the motion, or 'change' if a force changes it.
Get 1 point for the right answer, and 1 more point if you name the force, such as friction, gravity or a hand.
After every player has had 5 cards, add up the points.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Shuffle them and put them face down.
flow.say: In this game, every card is a moment. You say 'keep going' or 'change', and name the force if there is one.
flow.kid: Every card is a moment. Say 'keep going' or 'change'. Name the force if you can.

flow.do: Play one practice card together: the marble rolling onto a towel.
flow.say: Practice card. A marble rolls onto a towel. Keep going or change?
flow.kid: Practice card. A marble rolls onto a towel. Keep going or change? Tap your answer.

check.q: A marble rolls onto a towel. Keep going or change?
options: Keep going, because moving things keep moving
Change, because friction from the towel slows it down
check.why: Moving things do keep moving, unless a force acts. Here a force does act: friction from the towel's rough fibres slows the marble and soon stops it. That is why it is 'change'.

flow.do: Take turns until each player has had 5 cards. Keep score on the sheet.
flow.say: Your turn. Listen to the card. Keep going or change? Which force?
flow.kid: Listen to your card. Keep going or change? Name the force for an extra point.

flow.do: Add up the points. Ask which card was hardest.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which card was hardest? Why?

games.title: Bus Statues
games.context: This is a moving game. One person is the bus driver and calls out what the bus does. The others are passengers, and lean the way their bodies would really move.

printables.title: 12 driver cards
