The bus brakes suddenly.
The bus turns left.
The bus turns right.
The bus moves smoothly at a steady speed.
The bus goes over a speed breaker.
The bus stops at a signal.
The bus starts slowly and gently.
The bus hits a pothole and dips down.
The bus goes round a roundabout.
The bus is parked.
The driver brakes very gently.

printables.title: Passenger points
items: Passenger name
Right leans
Total

setup.art: Two children standing behind dining chairs, holding the chair backs like bus bars, while their mother holds a driver card.
setup.caption: 1. Passengers hold a chair back like a bus bar.

setup.art: The children leaning forward and freezing as the mother reads 'The bus brakes suddenly'.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the card. Lean the way your body would move. Freeze!

rules: Passengers stand with feet apart, holding the back of a chair as the bus bar.
The driver reads a card aloud.
Passengers lean the way their bodies would really move, and freeze like statues.
The driver checks: starting, lean back. Braking, lean forward. Turning left, lean right. Turning right, lean left. Steady speed or parked, stand still.
A right lean gets 1 point. After 12 cards, the passenger with most points becomes the driver.

flow.do: 1. Each passenger stands behind a chair and holds its back. 2. Shuffle the driver cards.
flow.say: You are passengers on a city bus. When I read a card, lean the way your body would really move, and freeze.
flow.kid: You are a passenger. Hold the chair like a bus bar. Lean the way your body would move. Freeze!
flow.parent: Keep leans small and gentle, and hold the chair all the time.

flow.do: Do one practice card: the bus brakes suddenly.
flow.say: Practice card. The bus brakes suddenly. Which way do you lean?
flow.kid: The bus brakes suddenly. Which way do you lean?

check.q: The bus brakes suddenly. Which way does a passenger lean?
options: Forward
Backward
Not at all
check.why: The passenger's body was moving forward with the bus, and it keeps moving forward when the bus slows down. So they lean forward. When the bus starts suddenly, it is the opposite: the body stays behind, so they lean back.

flow.do: Read the cards one by one. Check each lean and give points.
flow.say: Here comes the next card. Lean, and freeze!
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Lean. Freeze! Were you right?

flow.do: Ask which card fooled people most.
flow.say: Which card fooled you? Why does steady speed feel like standing still?
flow.kid: Which card fooled you? Why does a smooth ride feel still?

ask.q: Why does steady speed feel like standing still?
good: Nothing changes, so no force pushes you.
Your body moves along with the bus.

experiments.title: The Walking Drop: where will it land?
experiments.context: This is the main experiment of the unit. You walk past a target and let go of a pair of rolled socks right above it. Where do they land?
experiments.question: If I let go of a pair of rolled socks right above a plate while I am walking, where will they land? Does it change if I walk faster?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the socks land on the plate, before it, or past it? Will walking faster change where they land? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same socks, the same plate and the same height every time: hold the socks at chest height, arm out to the side. Only the walking speed changes: standing still, slow walk, fast walk. Do 3 tries at each speed, because one try can be a fluke. The helper always says 'now' when your hand is right above the plate.

materials.item: a pair of socks rolled into a tight ball, or a small cloth bag of rice tied shut (they don't bounce or roll away)
a steel plate or a paper circle about 20 cm across, as the target
3 coins or small paper squares, to mark where the socks land
a measuring tape, or a 30 cm ruler
a clear stretch of floor about 4 metres long, such as a hall or a corridor in the flat
a helper to watch from the side: a parent, a grandparent, a brother or sister

experiments.safety: Walk, never run. Clear toys and bags off the floor first, and don't do it on a wet floor.

schedule.what: Guess, then drop the socks over the plate while standing, walking slowly and walking fast. Measure where they land. Then try to hit the plate.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw two pictures: the path of the socks as you saw them, and as your helper saw them from the side.

setup.art: A tiled hall in a flat, with a steel plate on the floor in the middle and a girl standing about 3 metres away holding rolled socks at chest height, arm out to the side.
setup.caption: 1. Put the plate in the middle of the floor. Hold the socks at chest height.

setup.art: The girl walking past the plate, letting go of the socks just as her hand is above it, while her mother watches from the side and calls out.
setup.caption: 2. Walk past. Let go when your hand is right above the plate.

setup.art: Rolled socks lying on the floor past the plate, with a coin marking the spot and a measuring tape stretched from the plate to the coin.
setup.caption: 3. Mark where the socks land. Measure from the plate.

flow.do: 1. Put the plate in the middle of a clear floor. 2. Mark a starting line about 2 metres before the plate with a slipper. 3. Show your child how to hold the rolled socks: arm out to the side, at chest height.
flow.say: We are going to drop these socks right above the plate. First, you guess. If I let go right above the plate while I walk, where will the socks land? On it, before it, or past it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the plate on the floor. You will walk past it and let go of the socks. Where will they land? On the plate, before it, or past it? Why?

ask.q: Where will the socks land, and why do you think so?
good: Any guess with a reason is good. Many children say 'on the plate, because things fall straight down'. That is a fine guess to test.

flow.parent: Write down the guess and the reason before you start. Don't explain anything yet. Most children, and many grown-ups, guess the socks will land on the plate or just behind it.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands still with their hand right above the plate. 2. They let go. 3. Mark where the socks land with a coin, and measure from the edge of the plate nearest to the start.
flow.say: First, the easy one. Stand still, hold your hand above the plate, and let go. Where did they land?
flow.kid: Stand still. Hold the socks above the plate. Let go. Did they land on it?
flow.parent: Standing still, the socks should land on the plate. Write 0 cm. This is the result to compare with.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks slowly from the starting line, the way they walk round the flat. 2. You watch from the side and say 'now' when their hand is right above the plate. 3. They let go at 'now', and keep walking. 4. Mark and measure where the socks land. 5. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Now walk slowly past the plate. I'll say 'now' when your hand is right above it. Let go at 'now', and keep walking. Don't throw them, just open your hand.
flow.kid: Walk slowly past the plate. Let go when your helper says now. Just open your hand. Keep walking. Where did they land?
flow.parent: Expect the socks to land past the plate, often about 20 to 50 cm past, in the direction your child was walking. Measure from the plate to the middle of the socks. If they land on the plate, check that your child is not stopping or pulling the hand back as they let go.

check.q: Riya, a girl in Class 3, walks past a plate and lets go of rolled socks right above it. Where do the socks land?
options: On the plate
Before the plate, behind her
Past the plate, in the direction she was walking
check.why: The socks were moving forward with Riya. After she let go, nothing pushed them back, so they kept moving forward while they fell, and landed past the plate. Picking 'on the plate' means thinking the socks stop moving forward the moment they leave the hand. Picking 'behind her' means thinking the socks are left behind. Both are very common guesses.

flow.do: 1. Now your child walks fast, but does not run. 2. Say 'now' above the plate, as before. 3. Mark and measure. 4. Do it 3 times. 5. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Now walk fast, but don't run. Let go at 'now' again. Will the socks land in the same place, nearer the plate, or further away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Walk fast this time. Don't run! Let go when your helper says now. Do the socks land further away? Measure.
flow.parent: Walking fast, the socks usually land further past the plate, often 50 to 90 cm. Results vary by 10 or 20 cm between tries, because nobody lets go at exactly the same moment. That is why we do 3 tries.

flow.do: 1. Swap jobs: you walk and drop, and your child watches from the side, crouching low. 2. Ask them to watch the path of the socks in the air. 3. Then ask what the dropper saw.
flow.say: Now you watch from the side, and I'll walk. Watch the socks in the air very carefully. Do they fall straight down, or in a curve?
flow.kid: Now you watch from the side. Your helper walks and drops. Watch the socks in the air. Straight down, or a curve?

ask.q: What path did the socks take, seen from the side?
good: A curve, going forward and down.
Like a ball thrown gently forward.

ask.q: When you were the one walking, what did the socks seem to do?
good: They seemed to fall straight down beside my leg.
They stayed next to me as they fell.

flow.parent: Seen from the side, the socks fall in a forward curve. The person walking sees them fall almost straight down beside their leg, because the socks keep up with them. Both are true views of the same fall.

flow.do: Challenge your child to make the socks land on the plate while walking slowly. Give 3 tries.
flow.say: Here is a challenge. Can you walk slowly and make the socks land on the plate? When should you let go?
flow.kid: Can you make the socks land on the plate while you walk? When will you let go?
flow.parent: The trick is to let go before your hand reaches the plate, about one big step early at a slow walk. Children who work this out on their own have understood the idea. Aid workers dropping food parcels from planes must let go long before the plane is over the target, for the same reason.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: when you let go of something while you walk, it keeps moving forward as it falls. What I saw: standing still, the socks landed on the plate. Walking slowly, they landed about 35 cm past. Walking fast, about 70 cm past. Why: the socks were moving forward with me, and nothing pushed them back after I let go, so they kept going forward until they hit the floor.

experiments.title: The Egg That Keeps Turning
experiments.context: In this experiment you find out which eggs are raw and which are boiled, without cracking any of them. You spin each egg, stop it for a moment, and let go.
experiments.question: Can we tell a raw egg from a boiled egg by spinning it, stopping it and letting go?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When you stop a spinning egg with one finger and let go, will it stay still or start turning again? Will a raw egg and a boiled egg do the same thing? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use eggs of about the same size, spun on the same plate. Stop each one with one fingertip for about one second, then lift your finger. Test each egg 3 times. You don't know which egg is which until the end, so you can't fool yourself.
results_table: Easy or hard to spin fast?
Starts turning again after I stop it? Try 1

materials.item: 4 eggs of about the same size: 2 hard-boiled and cooled, and 2 raw
a large flat steel plate or a tray
a pencil, to write A, B, C and D on the eggs
a bowl, to crack one egg into at the end

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the eggs and cools them in cold water before the child touches them. Wash hands with soap after touching raw eggs. If your family does not use eggs, do the Water That Keeps Turning activity instead (a2). It shows the same idea.

schedule.what: A grown-up boils 2 eggs and mixes them with 2 raw ones. Spin, stop and release each egg. Guess which are raw. Check by cracking one.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the inside of a raw egg and a boiled egg, and show with arrows what keeps turning.

setup.art: Four white eggs marked A, B, C and D in pencil, sitting on a steel plate on a kitchen counter.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up mixes up 2 boiled and 2 raw eggs and marks them A to D.

setup.art: A child's hand twisting an egg lying on its side so that it spins on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 2. Spin an egg on its side on the plate.

setup.art: A fingertip resting lightly on top of a spinning egg to stop it, then lifting away, with curved arrows showing the egg turning again.
setup.caption: 3. Stop it with one finger for a second. Let go. Watch.

flow.do: 1. Before your child comes in, hard-boil 2 eggs for about 10 minutes and cool them in cold water. 2. Mix them with 2 raw eggs of the same size. 3. Write A, B, C and D on them in pencil. 4. Note secretly which are raw.
flow.say: I have 4 eggs. Two are boiled and two are raw, and only I know which. Can you find out without cracking them?
flow.kid: Here are 4 eggs, A, B, C and D. Two are raw. Two are boiled. Can you find out which, without cracking them?
flow.parent: Boil the eggs well ahead, so they are fully cooled. Warm eggs would give the answer away. Keep the note of which is which out of sight.

flow.do: 1. Lay egg A on its side on the plate. 2. Show your child how to spin it with a quick twist of the fingers. 3. Spin each egg once. Is it easy or hard to spin fast?
flow.say: Spin each egg on its side. Do they all spin the same way? Is any of them harder to spin fast?
flow.kid: Spin each egg on its side, on the plate. Does one wobble? Is one harder to spin? Write it down.
flow.parent: A boiled egg spins fast and smoothly. A raw egg is harder to spin fast and often wobbles, because its runny inside does not turn at once with the shell. Keep spins gentle, so no egg flies off the plate.

flow.do: 1. Spin egg A. 2. Touch the top of it with one fingertip, just long enough to stop it, about one second. 3. Lift your finger at once. 4. Watch for 3 seconds. Does it stay still or start turning again? 5. Do 3 tries for each egg and fill in the table.
flow.say: Now the real test. Spin the egg, stop it with one finger, and let go straight away. Watch it closely. What do you think a raw egg will do? Why?
flow.kid: Spin the egg. Stop it with one finger. Let go at once. Does it stay still? Or does it start turning again? Try each egg 3 times.
flow.parent: A boiled egg stays still once stopped. A raw egg slowly starts turning again, for half a turn or more. If nothing happens with any egg, the stop was too long: touch for only about one second, then lift your finger right away.

check.q: Meera, a girl in Chennai, stops a spinning raw egg with her finger and lets go. The egg starts turning again. Why?
options: Her finger pushed it
The runny inside kept turning after the shell stopped, and it turned the shell again
Raw eggs are lighter
check.why: Meera's finger stopped only the shell. The runny inside was not touched, so it kept turning, because of inertia. When she let go, the turning inside rubbed on the shell and set it turning again. In a boiled egg the inside is solid and fixed to the shell, so the whole egg stops together. Picking 'her finger pushed it' is a fair guess: try lifting the finger very carefully, straight up, and see that it still happens.

flow.do: 1. Your child says which eggs they think are raw and why. 2. Show your secret note. 3. Crack one egg your child chose as raw into a bowl, to check.
flow.say: Which two do you think are raw? What did they do that tells you? Let's check one by cracking it.
flow.kid: Which two eggs are raw? Say why. Now crack one into a bowl. Were you right?
flow.parent: Use the raw egg for cooking afterwards, so it isn't wasted. Wash hands with soap after touching raw eggs.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the runny inside of a raw egg keeps turning when the shell is stopped. What I saw: eggs B and D started turning again after I stopped them, 3 times out of 3. Eggs A and C stayed still. B was raw when we cracked it. Why: my finger stopped only the shell, and the inside kept moving because of inertia, so it turned the shell again.

experiments.title: How Far Will It Roll? On the way to ice
experiments.context: In this experiment you roll a marble down the same ramp onto three different floors, and measure how far it goes. It shows why moving things on Earth stop.
experiments.question: A marble rolls down the same ramp onto a towel, a doormat and a bare floor. On which will it roll furthest, and why?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the three surfaces in order, from shortest roll to longest roll. Then guess: on ice, would it roll even further? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same marble, the same ramp at the same height, and let go from the same mark every time. Don't push the marble, just let go. Only the surface changes. Roll 3 times on each, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a glass marble (goli), or a small hard ball
a 30 cm ruler with a groove down the middle, as the ramp
a book about 3 cm thick, to rest one end of the ruler on
a bath towel spread flat, and a doormat or a rug
a bare, smooth floor: tiles, mosaic or stone
a measuring tape, and a coin to mark where the marble stops

experiments.safety: Pick up the marble after each roll so nobody slips on it. Keep marbles away from children under 3.

schedule.what: Roll a marble down a ruler ramp onto a towel, a doormat and a bare floor. Measure how far it rolls. Imagine ice.

experiments.record: Fill in the table and draw a bar chart with one bar for each surface.

setup.art: A 30 cm ruler with one end resting on a book and the other on the floor, a marble held at the top of its groove.
setup.caption: 1. Rest one end of the ruler on a book to make a ramp.

setup.art: A marble rolling off the end of a ruler ramp onto a flat bath towel on the floor, stopping after a short distance.
setup.caption: 2. Put the end of the ramp on the towel. Let the marble go from the top.

setup.art: A measuring tape on a tiled floor from the end of the ruler ramp to a coin where the marble stopped, much further away than on the towel.
setup.caption: 3. Mark where it stops. Measure from the end of the ramp.

flow.do: 1. Rest one end of the ruler on the book. 2. Lay the towel flat so the low end of the ruler touches it. 3. Mark a starting line near the top of the ruler with a pencil.
flow.say: We'll roll this marble down the same ramp onto three floors: a towel, a doormat and the bare floor. Which will it roll furthest on? Which shortest? Why?
flow.kid: Make a ramp with the ruler and a book. Which floor will the marble roll furthest on? The towel, the mat or the bare floor? Why?

ask.q: Put the three surfaces in order, and say why.
good: Towel shortest, then the mat, then the floor, because the towel is rough and the floor is smooth.
Any order with a reason is a good guess.

flow.do: 1. Hold the marble at the starting line and let go, without pushing. 2. Mark where it stops with a coin. 3. Measure from the end of the ruler to the coin. 4. Do 3 rolls on each surface. 5. Write each one in the table.
flow.say: Let go of the marble at the line. Don't push it. Where did it stop? Let's measure, then do it again.
flow.kid: Let go of the marble at the line. No pushing! Put a coin where it stops. Measure. Do 3 rolls on each floor.
flow.parent: On a towel, the marble may stop within 10 to 30 cm. On a mat, a little further. On smooth tiles it can roll 2 metres or more, sometimes all the way to the wall. If it reaches the wall, write 'reached the wall' and lower the ramp to half a book, then do all three surfaces again at that height.

flow.do: 1. Find the middle result for each surface: the one between the smallest and the biggest. 2. Compare them.
flow.say: Which surface slowed the marble most? Which slowed it least? What do you think slowed it down?
flow.kid: Which floor stopped the marble fastest? What slowed it down?

check.q: Arjun's marble rolled 20 cm on a towel and 250 cm on tiles, from the same ramp. Why did it go so much further on the tiles?
options: The tiles pushed it along
The tiles gave less friction, so less force slowed it down
It was going faster at the start on the tiles
check.why: The marble left the ramp at the same speed both times. The towel's rough fibres gave a lot of friction, which slowed it quickly. The smooth tiles gave much less friction, so it kept moving much longer. Nothing pushed it along. Moving things keep moving by themselves, and friction is what stops them.

flow.do: Ask your child to imagine smoother and smoother floors. First ice, then something even more slippery. Last, a floor with no friction and no air.
flow.say: On ice, the marble would slide much further than on tiles. What if the floor were even more slippery than ice? And what if there were no friction and no air at all?
flow.kid: Imagine a floor of ice. Then one even more slippery. Then one with no friction and no air. How far would the marble roll?

ask.q: With no friction and no air at all, how far would the marble roll?
good: It would never stop, because nothing would slow it.

flow.parent: This is the step that matters most. The pattern in your table points to it: less friction, longer roll. With nothing at all to slow it, the marble would keep rolling for ever. That is Newton's first law, worked out from your own results.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: friction is what slows a rolling marble down, and with no friction it would never stop. What I saw: from the same ramp, the marble rolled about 20 cm on the towel, 60 cm on the mat and 250 cm on the tiles. Why: the rougher the surface, the more friction, and the faster it stopped. Less friction means a longer roll, so with none it would keep going.

activities.title: The Coin That Stays Behind
activities.context: This is a quick trick to start the unit. A coin sits on a card on top of a tumbler. You pull the card away slowly, then fast. Where does the coin go?

materials.item: a steel or plastic tumbler
a square of stiff card about 8 cm across, cut from a cereal or medicine box, or a playing card
a five-rupee or ten-rupee coin
a second coin of the same kind

activities.safety: Flick the card sideways, not towards anyone's face.
activities.record: Write 'slow pull' and 'fast flick', and draw where the coin went each time.

setup.art: A steel tumbler with a square of card on top and a coin in the middle of the card.
setup.caption: 1. Put the card on the tumbler and the coin on the card.

setup.art: A finger flicking the card sideways off the tumbler, the card flying away, and the coin dropping into the tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Flick the card away fast, sideways. Where does the coin go?

flow.do: 1. Put the card on the tumbler and the coin in the middle of the card. 2. Your child pulls the card slowly sideways off the tumbler.
flow.say: Pull the card away slowly, sideways. What happens to the coin?
flow.kid: Pull the card away slowly. Watch the coin. Where did it go?
flow.parent: The coin should slide along with the card and fall off beside the tumbler, or stay on the card.

flow.do: 1. Set it up again. 2. Before the flick, ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Your child flicks the edge of the card hard and fast with a finger, straight sideways. 4. Try 5 times, then with two coins stacked.
flow.say: Now, before you flick it fast, guess. Where will the coin go this time? Why do you think so? Now flick it hard, straight sideways.
flow.kid: Set it up again. Guess first: where will the coin go? Now flick the card hard and fast. Was your guess right?
flow.parent: Flicking the card with a fingernail, the way you flick a carrom coin, works best. Most flicks drop the coin into the tumbler. If the coin flies off, the flick was upwards: flick straight along the top of the tumbler. Two stacked coins usually drop in even more surely, because they have more mass.

flow.do: Talk about what happened. Don't give the answer before your child has tried to explain it.
flow.say: Nothing pushed the coin into the tumbler. So why did it end up inside?
flow.kid: Nothing pushed the coin down. So why did it fall into the tumbler?

check.q: Kavya flicks the card away fast, and the coin drops into the tumbler. Why?
options: The flick pushed the coin down
The coin stayed still while the card shot away, and then gravity pulled it down
The coin is magnetic
check.why: The coin was still, and it stayed still, because the card rubbed on it for only a tiny moment. That was too short to get it moving. With the card gone, gravity pulled the coin straight down. With a slow pull, the card rubs on the coin for longer, so the coin moves with it. Things at rest stay at rest until a force has time to move them. This is inertia.

activities.title: The Water That Keeps Turning
activities.context: In this activity you stir water in a bowl and stop stirring. Does the water stop too? Then you turn the bowl and watch a leaf on the water. It works for families who do not use eggs, instead of the egg experiment.

materials.item: a round steel bowl, about half full of water
a spoon
a pinch of tea leaves or jeera seeds, so you can see the water move
a small leaf, such as a tulsi or curry leaf, or a matchstick

activities.safety: Do it on the kitchen counter or the floor, with a cloth under the bowl for spills.
activities.record: Draw the bowl from above with arrows showing how the water moved after you took the spoon out.

setup.art: A steel bowl of water with tea leaves swirling round, and a spoon being lifted out.
setup.caption: 1. Stir the water fast in a circle. Take the spoon out. Watch the tea leaves.

setup.art: A curry leaf floating on still water in a round bowl. Two hands turn the bowl a quarter turn, and the leaf still points the same way.
setup.caption: 2. Float a leaf. Turn the bowl quickly. Does the leaf turn with it?

flow.do: 1. Put the bowl on the counter and add a pinch of tea leaves. 2. Your child stirs fast in a circle for 10 strokes. 3. They lift the spoon out. 4. Count how many seconds the tea leaves keep going round.
flow.say: Stir the water fast, then lift the spoon out. Will the water stop when the spoon stops? Why? Let's count how long it keeps going.
flow.kid: Stir the water fast. Lift the spoon out. Does the water stop? Count the seconds it keeps turning.
flow.parent: The water usually keeps turning for 15 seconds or more, slowing down little by little. Friction with the bowl slowly stops it.

flow.do: 1. Wait until the water is completely still. 2. Float the leaf in the middle, pointing at a spot on the wall. 3. Your child turns the bowl quickly a quarter turn, then holds it still.
flow.say: Now the water is still. If you turn the bowl quickly, will the water and the leaf turn with it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Wait until the water is still. Float the leaf. Turn the bowl quickly. Does the leaf turn with the bowl?
flow.parent: The bowl turns, but the water and the leaf mostly stay where they were, so the leaf keeps pointing at nearly the same spot on the wall. Turn it smoothly and quickly. A slow turn gives the bowl time to drag the water round.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain both results.
flow.say: The moving water kept moving, and the still water stayed still. What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Moving water kept moving. Still water stayed still. Why?

check.q: Lakshmi stirs water in a bowl and lifts the spoon out. Why does the water keep turning?
options: Because of inertia: moving water keeps moving until friction slows it
Because the bowl is still turning
Because the tea leaves are pushing it
check.why: The moving water keeps moving because nothing has stopped it yet. Friction with the bowl slowly takes its motion away. The bowl is not turning, and the tea leaves are only carried along. They just help you see the water move.

activities.title: The Carrom Tower
activities.context: In this activity you build a tower of carrom coins and knock out only the bottom one. It shows that still things stay still when a force acts on them for only a moment.

materials.item: a carrom board with its coins and striker, or 6 coins of the same kind and a 30 cm ruler on a smooth table
a little carrom powder, if you have it

activities.safety: Keep fingers out of the way of the striker.
activities.record: Write how many tries it took to knock out only the bottom coin, and draw the tower before and after.

setup.art: A tower of six carrom coins stacked on a carrom board, and a striker placed flat on the board a hand-width away, aimed at the bottom coin.
setup.caption: 1. Stack 6 coins. Aim the striker at the bottom one.

setup.art: The bottom coin shooting out sideways while the other five coins drop down straight, still in a tower.
setup.caption: 2. Flick hard. The bottom coin shoots out. The rest drop down.

flow.do: 1. Stack 6 coins in a neat tower in the middle of the board. 2. Put the striker flat on the board about 15 cm away, aimed at the bottom coin.
flow.say: If you hit the bottom coin hard, what will the rest of the tower do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make a tower of 6 coins. Aim the striker at the bottom one. What will the tower do? Guess first.
flow.parent: No carrom board? Use 6 coins of the same kind on a smooth table. Slide the edge of a ruler fast along the table into the bottom coin.

flow.do: 1. Your child flicks the striker hard into the bottom coin. 2. Try a soft, slow flick too. 3. Try 5 times each.
flow.say: Flick it hard and fast. Then try a slow, soft flick. What is different?
flow.kid: Flick the striker hard. Did only the bottom coin move? Now try a slow flick. What happened?
flow.parent: A hard, fast hit knocks out the bottom coin, and the rest drop straight down. A slow hit pushes the whole tower over. Hitting low and flat matters, so it may take a few tries.

flow.do: Talk about why the fast hit works.
flow.say: Why did the coins on top drop straight down instead of flying off?
flow.kid: Why did the top coins stay and drop down?

ask.q: Why did the top coins stay?
good: They were still and stayed still, because the bottom coin rubbed them for only a moment.

activities.title: Tumbler on a Tray: start, stop and turn
activities.context: In this activity you move a tray with a tumbler of water on it, starting, stopping and turning suddenly. You see which way the water slops, and why.

materials.item: a steel tumbler about half full of water
a tray or a big steel plate
a kitchen towel spread on the floor or table

activities.safety: Do it over the towel. Move the tray only a short way, and gently at first.

schedule.what: Tumbler on a Tray: start, stop and turn

activities.record: Draw the tray and tumbler three times: starting, stopping and turning. Show with an arrow which way the water slopped.

setup.art: A tumbler of water on a tray held by two small hands, the tray pulled forward suddenly and the water tilted up at the back of the tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. Pull the tray forward suddenly. Which way does the water slop?

setup.art: The same tray stopped suddenly and the water tilted up at the front of the tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Move it smoothly, then stop suddenly. Which way now?

flow.do: 1. Put the tumbler in the middle of the tray. 2. Your child holds the tray still, then pulls it forward suddenly, a short way.
flow.say: Guess first. If you pull the tray forward suddenly, which way will the water slop? Why?
flow.kid: Hold the tray still. Guess: which way will the water slop? Now pull the tray forward suddenly.
flow.parent: The water rises at the back of the tumbler, because the still water stays behind for a moment while the tumbler moves off.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks slowly with the tray, then stops suddenly. 2. Then they walk and turn a corner.
flow.say: Now walk slowly with the tray and stop suddenly. Which way does the water go? And when you turn a corner?
flow.kid: Walk slowly. Stop suddenly. Which way did the water go? Now turn a corner. Which way now?
flow.parent: When the tray stops, the water slops forward, because it keeps moving. When the tray turns, the water rises on the outside of the turn, because it keeps going straight.

flow.do: Connect it to a bus or an auto.
flow.say: When the bus brakes suddenly, which way do the passengers lurch? Is that like the water?
flow.kid: When a bus brakes, which way do people lurch? Why? Is it like the water?

check.q: Farhan is standing in a city bus. The bus brakes suddenly. Which way does his body lurch?
options: Forward, because his body keeps moving
Backward, because the bus pushes him back
He does not move at all
check.why: Farhan's body was moving forward with the bus. When the bus slows, his body keeps moving forward until his feet, the floor and his hand on the bar slow him down. That is why people hold the bar. Picking 'backward' mixes it up with what happens when the bus starts suddenly.

activities.title: Toss It on a Moving Train, Metro or Lift
activities.context: In this activity you toss a soft ball straight up while you travel in a train, a metro or a lift. Does it fall behind you? Do it next time you travel.

materials.item: a small soft ball, or a pair of rolled socks
a train, metro or lift journey with a grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up is with you all the time. Stay seated in a train or metro, toss the ball only a little way up, and do it only while the ride is smooth. Never lean out of a window or a door.

schedule.what: Toss It on a Moving Train, Metro or Lift

activities.record: Write where you were, and where the ball landed when the ride was smooth, and when it braked or turned.

setup.art: A girl sitting in a metro coach with her mother, tossing a rolled pair of socks a little way up, with buildings blurring past the window.
setup.caption: 1. While the ride is smooth, toss the ball a little way straight up.

setup.art: The socks landing back in the girl's open hand, with an arrow showing they went straight up and down.
setup.caption: 2. Does it land back in your hand, or behind you?

flow.do: Wait until the train, metro or lift is moving smoothly at a steady speed. Your child, sitting, tosses the ball a little way straight up.
flow.say: Guess first. The train is moving fast. If you toss the ball straight up, will it land in your hand or behind you? Why?
flow.kid: Wait until the ride is smooth. Guess: will the ball fall behind you? Toss it a little way up. Where did it land?
flow.parent: It lands back in the hand, as it would at home. The ball was moving with the train before it was tossed, and it keeps that forward motion in the air.

flow.do: Try again just as the train slows down for a station, or as the lift starts or stops.
flow.say: Now try as the train slows down. Does the ball still land in your hand?
flow.kid: Try again as the train slows down. Where does the ball land now?
flow.parent: As the train slows, the ball keeps its speed while the train and your hand slow down, so it lands a little ahead, towards the front of the train. In a lift, you feel the push only as it starts and stops.

flow.do: Talk about it on the way home.
flow.say: With your eyes shut on a smooth ride, could you tell you were moving? So could we be moving right now, without feeling it?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes on a smooth ride. Can you tell you are moving? Is the Earth moving now?

ask.q: Why don't we feel the Earth moving?
good: Because it moves smoothly, and we move with it.
Like a smooth train, everything around us moves with us.

activities.title: The Dough Passenger
activities.context: In this activity you make a small atta-dough passenger, give them a ride on a toy car, and crash the car gently into a book. Then you give them a seatbelt.

materials.item: a toy car or a small toy truck
a lump of atta dough the size of a lemon, or play dough
a rubber band
a tray or a board, and 2 books, to make a slope
a heavy book, as a wall at the bottom

activities.safety: Use only a gentle slope, and keep the dough out of the toy car's wheels.
activities.record: Draw where the passenger landed without a seatbelt and with one.

setup.art: A small atta-dough figure sitting on a toy car at the top of a tray propped on two books, with a heavy book as a wall at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Seat the dough passenger on the car at the top of the slope.

setup.art: The toy car stopped against the book, the dough figure flying forward off it.
setup.caption: 2. Let the car roll into the book. Where does the passenger go?

setup.art: The same car against the book, with a rubber band holding the dough figure safely on.
setup.caption: 3. Add a rubber band seatbelt. Try again.

flow.do: 1. Make a small dough person and press them gently onto the top of the toy car. 2. Prop one end of the tray on 2 books. 3. Put the heavy book across the bottom as a wall.
flow.say: Our dough passenger is going for a ride. When the car hits the book wall, what will happen to the passenger? Why?
flow.kid: Make a dough person. Seat them on the car. When the car hits the book, what will happen to them?

flow.do: Let the car roll down the slope into the book. Do it 3 times, and mark where the passenger lands each time.
flow.say: Let the car go. Don't push it. Where did the passenger land?
flow.kid: Let the car roll down. No pushing! Where did the passenger land? Try 3 times.
flow.parent: The car stops at the book, but the passenger keeps moving and flies off the front. That is inertia.

flow.do: Stretch the rubber band round the car and across the passenger. Roll it 3 times again.
flow.say: Now let's give the passenger a seatbelt. What do you think will happen this time?
flow.kid: Put a rubber band over the passenger. That is their seatbelt. Roll the car again.
flow.parent: Now the passenger stays on. The rubber band gives the force that stops the passenger along with the car.

flow.do: Connect it to real seatbelts and helmets.
flow.say: Why does everyone in a car need to wear a seatbelt, even in the back seat?
flow.kid: Why should everyone in a car wear a seatbelt, even at the back?

check.q: A car brakes hard. Why does a passenger without a seatbelt move forward?
options: The seat pushes them forward
Their body keeps moving at the old speed until something stops it
The brakes pull them forward
check.why: The brakes stop the car, but nothing is holding the passenger, so their body keeps moving forward at the old speed. Without a seatbelt, the seat in front or the windscreen stops them, and that hurts. A seatbelt stops them along with the car, more gently. That is why Indian road rules ask everyone in a car to wear one, front and back.

activities.title: Swing It and Let Go
activities.context: In this activity you swing a sock on a string in a circle and let go. Does it keep going round, or fly off straight?

materials.item: a soft sock with a knot tied in it
a string about 60 cm long, tied to the sock
a strip of newspaper or chalk marks on the floor, to mark where it lands

activities.safety: Do it in an open space, with nobody near you and nothing breakable around. Swing low and slowly. A grown-up watches.
activities.record: Draw the circle from above, and a line showing the way the sock flew off.

setup.art: A girl in an empty room swinging a sock on a string in a slow, low circle beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Swing the sock in a slow circle, low down.

setup.art: A drawing from above: the circle path, and a straight dotted line going off along the edge of the circle where the sock was let go.
setup.caption: 2. Let go of the string. Which way does the sock fly?

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the end of the string and swings the sock in a slow, low circle. 2. Ask what the string is doing to the sock.
flow.say: Swing it slowly. What is the string doing to the sock all the time?
flow.kid: Swing the sock slowly, low down. Can you feel the string pulling?
flow.parent: The string pulls the sock towards the hand all the time. That pull keeps turning it round the circle.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess. 2. Your child lets go of the string as the sock passes in front of them. 3. Try 3 times.
flow.say: Guess first. When you let go, will the sock keep curving, or fly off straight? Why?
flow.kid: Guess: will the sock keep curving? Let go of the string. Which way did it fly?
flow.parent: It flies off in a straight line, the way it was moving at that moment. It does not keep curving, because nothing is turning it any more.

flow.do: Talk about it.
flow.say: Why did the sock go straight once you let go?
flow.kid: Why did the sock fly straight?

good: The string stopped pulling, so nothing turned it.
Moving things go straight unless a force turns them.

projects.title: Build a Balloon Hover Puck
projects.context: In this 2-day project you build a puck that floats on a thin layer of air from a balloon. With almost no friction, one gentle tap sends it gliding a long way, like a ball on ice.

materials.item: an old CD or DVD
a push-pull cap from a water bottle or a squash bottle
a round balloon
a strong glue such as Fevikwik, or a glue gun used by a grown-up, or Prestik putty
a smooth table or a tiled floor
a measuring tape

projects.safety: A grown-up uses the glue. Keep glue off fingers. Don't put a burst balloon in the mouth.

schedule.what: Glue the push-pull cap onto the CD and leave it to dry.
Fit the balloon, test the hover puck, and compare it with a plain CD.

projects.record: Write how far the plain CD slid and how far the hover puck glided, from the same tap, 3 times each.

setup.art: Two hands gluing a push-pull bottle cap over the hole in the middle of a CD.
setup.caption: 1. Glue the bottle cap over the hole of the CD.

setup.art: A blown-up balloon stretched over the closed push-pull cap on the CD.
setup.caption: 2. Blow up the balloon and fit it over the closed cap.

setup.art: The CD with its balloon gliding across a tiled floor after the cap is pulled open, with a long arrow ahead of it.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the cap open. Tap it gently. How far does it glide?

flow.do: 1. A grown-up glues the push-pull cap over the hole in the middle of one CD, with no gaps around the edge. 2. Leave it to dry overnight.
flow.say: Today we build the puck. Tomorrow we test it. The air from the balloon will come out under the CD. What do you think that will do?
flow.kid: Today you build the puck. A grown-up glues the cap onto the CD. Leave it to dry.
flow.parent: The seal must be airtight, or the air leaks out of the sides instead of under the CD. Prestik pressed all round the cap works if you have no glue.

flow.do: 1. Close the push-pull cap. 2. Blow up the balloon, twist its neck, and stretch it over the cap. 3. Put the puck on the floor and pull the cap open. 4. Give it one gentle tap.
flow.say: Pull the cap open, wait until you hear the air, and give it one gentle tap. How far does it go?
flow.kid: Close the cap. Put the balloon on it. Open the cap. Tap the puck gently. Where does it stop?
flow.parent: With air flowing, the puck glides far and smoothly, often across the whole room, until the balloon runs out. Use the same small tap each time.

flow.do: 1. Tap the plain CD with no balloon, with the same small tap. 2. Measure how far each one went. 3. Do 3 tries each.
flow.say: Now tap the plain CD the same way. Which went further? Why?
flow.kid: Tap the plain CD the same way. Measure. Which one went further? Why?
flow.parent: The plain CD rubs on the floor and stops within a few centimetres. The hover puck rides on air, so friction is almost gone. This is how an air hockey table works.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: when friction is almost gone, a moving thing keeps going a long way. What I saw: the plain CD slid about 10 cm. The hover puck glided about 3 metres from the same tap. Why: the air lifted the puck off the floor, so almost nothing slowed it down.

challenges.title: Save the Dough Passenger
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You design a car that keeps a dough passenger safe when it crashes into a book from a steeper slope.
challenges.problem: A toy car rolls down a steep slope and hits a book wall. Design a way to keep a soft atta-dough passenger on the car and unsquashed.
constraints: The slope must be propped on at least 3 books.
The passenger must stay on the car, and keep their shape, in 3 tries out of 3.
materials: cotton wool, a sponge or folded cloth
general: A seatbelt made from a rubber band.
A soft bumper on the front of the car, such as a sponge, so the car stops more slowly.
A seat with a high back and sides, made from cardboard.
creative: A crumple zone: a folded paper box on the front of the car that squashes and makes the stop gentler.
An air bag: a small balloon, half blown up, taped in front of the passenger.
A soft wall instead of a hard book: does that help as much as changing the car?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to save the passenger. Draw it, build it, and test it 3 times. Which part helped most?

setup.art: A tray propped on three books, a toy car with a dough passenger at the top, and a book wall at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Make a steep slope with a book wall at the bottom.

setup.art: A toy car with a sponge bumper, a cardboard seat and a rubber band seatbelt holding a dough figure.
setup.caption: 2. Add your safety ideas to the car.

setup.art: The car stopped against the book, the dough passenger still sitting on it, unsquashed.
setup.caption: 3. Test it 3 times. Is the passenger safe?

flow.do: Run the car with a bare passenger down the steep slope once, so your child sees the problem.
flow.say: Watch what happens to the passenger with no safety at all. What goes wrong?
flow.kid: Roll the car with no safety. What happens to the passenger?

flow.do: Your child draws a design, then builds it from home materials.
flow.say: What will keep the passenger on? What will make the stop gentler? Draw your idea first, then build it.
flow.kid: Draw your idea first. Then build it. Keep the passenger on. Make the stop gentle.

flow.do: Test it 3 times, and improve it after each try.
flow.say: Test it. Did the passenger stay on? Were they squashed? What will you change?
flow.kid: Test it 3 times. Did the passenger stay safe? Change one thing and try again.
flow.parent: A seatbelt keeps the passenger on. A soft bumper or crumple zone makes the car stop over a longer distance, so the passenger is stopped more gently. Real cars use both.

challenges.title: The Longest Glide
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You make a thing that glides as far as possible across the floor after one push, by beating friction.
challenges.problem: Make a small thing that goes as far as possible across a tiled floor after one gentle push from a ruler held at the same height each time.
constraints: The push is always the same: a ruler pulled back to the same mark and let go, like a catapult, or one gentle push with the same flick.
It must carry one coin as its load.
materials: a steel plate, a plastic lid, a tray
general: Put wheels under it: round pencils or bottle caps on straws.
Put it on marbles, which roll like ball bearings.
Make the bottom very smooth and flat.
creative: A lid on four marbles held in place with bottle caps.
Rub a little cooking oil or talcum powder on the bottom of a steel plate, then wipe the floor afterwards.
Make it heavier or lighter: does that change how far it goes?
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own glider. Test it 3 times, measure, and change one thing at a time.

setup.art: A plastic lid resting on four marbles on a tiled floor, with a coin on top and a ruler ready to push it.
setup.caption: 1. Build a glider that will carry one coin.

setup.art: A measuring tape along the floor from a start line to where the lid glider stopped.
setup.caption: 2. Push it the same way each time. Measure how far it goes.

flow.do: Push a plain steel plate with a coin on it, using the same push. Measure how far it goes.
flow.say: This is our starting result. The plate rubs on the floor. How could we make it go further?
flow.kid: Push a plain plate with the same push. Measure. How can you make it go further?

flow.do: Your child builds a glider and tests it.
flow.say: What slows the plate down? How can you make less of it?
flow.kid: What slows the plate down? Build a glider with less friction. Test it.
flow.parent: Friction is what slows it. Rolling on marbles or wheels gives much less friction than sliding. Children often discover this on their own.

flow.do: Test 3 times and compare with the plain plate.
flow.say: How much further did your glider go than the plain plate? Why?
flow.kid: Measure 3 tries. How much further than the plain plate? Why?

videos.title: Can You Drop A Ball From A Moving Vehicle And Have It Land Straight Down?
videos.why: A football fired backwards from a fast truck at exactly the truck's speed drops almost straight down. It is the walking drop turned the other way round.
videos.check: Id and title confirmed through YouTube's public oEmbed lookup (channel MythBusters). Not watched from here: a parent should preview it, check its length and talk about why stunts with vehicles are only for trained teams.

quiz.p: Which sentence says Newton's first law?
opts: A moving thing always slows down by itself
A thing stays still, or keeps moving straight at the same speed, until a force changes it
quiz.why: This is the first law. The first option is the old, wrong idea. Moving things slow down only when a force, such as friction, acts on them.

quiz.p: A coin sits on a card on a tumbler. You flick the card away fast. What does the coin do?
quiz.why: The coin stays still because of inertia, and then gravity pulls it down into the tumbler. It does not fly with the card, because the flick rubs it for too short a time.

quiz.p: Nisha walks past a plate and lets go of rolled socks right above it. Where do they land?
quiz.why: The socks keep moving forward as they fall, so they land past the plate. Picking 'on the plate' means thinking they lose their forward motion when they leave her hand.

quiz.p: In the walking drop, what happens when you walk faster?
opts: The socks land further past the plate
The socks land on the plate
quiz.why: Walking faster gives the socks more forward speed, so they travel further forward while they fall.

quiz.p: Why does a rolling marble stop sooner on a towel than on tiles?
quiz.why: The towel's rough fibres give more friction, which slows the marble. On smooth tiles there is less friction, so it rolls further.

quiz.p: A stone is slid across smooth ice. Why does it go so far?
opts: Ice gives very little friction to slow it
quiz.why: Ice is very slippery, so there is very little friction. With little to slow it, the stone keeps moving a long way.

quiz.p: Why should everyone in a car wear a seatbelt?
opts: When the car stops suddenly, their body keeps moving forward, and the belt stops them safely
It keeps the car from moving
It makes the car go faster
quiz.why: In a sudden stop, a passenger's body keeps its speed. The seatbelt gives the force that stops them along with the car, instead of the seat in front or the windscreen.

quiz.p: A bus brakes suddenly. Which way does water in a tumbler on the seat slop?
quiz.why: The water keeps moving forward while the tumbler slows with the bus, so it slops forward.

quiz.p: Why can't we feel the Earth moving?
opts: It moves smoothly and steadily, and we move with it
quiz.why: The Earth moves very fast, but smoothly. Like a ball in a smooth train, everything moves with us, so we feel nothing.

quiz.p: Aryabhata said the stars seem to move west because the Earth turns. What did he compare this to?
opts: A person in a moving boat, who sees the trees on the bank move backwards
quiz.why: Aryabhata wrote this comparison around 499 CE, in his book the Aryabhatiya.

quiz.p: Pierre Gassendi dropped stones from the top of a moving ship's mast in 1640. What did he find?
opts: They landed at the foot of the mast
quiz.why: The stones kept the ship's forward motion while they fell, so they landed at the foot of the mast. This showed a moving Earth would not leave falling things behind.

quiz.p: You stop a spinning raw egg for a second and let go. What happens?
quiz.why: The runny inside keeps turning when the shell is stopped, because of inertia. When you let go, it turns the shell again.

quiz.p: What do scientists still not know about inertia?
opts: Why things have inertia at all
quiz.why: Inertia has been measured very exactly, and the law always works. But why mass resists changes in motion is still argued about.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3 in Kochi, writes down six moments from her day. Sort each one: is a force changing the motion, or is the thing just keeping on doing what it was doing?
cats: It keeps doing what it was doing
items: A football she kicks starts rolling
A force changes the motion
Her pencil box lies on the desk all morning
It keeps doing what it was doing
Her cycle slows down when she stops pedalling
A force changes the motion
A spacecraft far out in space keeps moving with its engines off
It keeps doing what it was doing
Her hand catches a tossed ball
A force changes the motion
A puck glides straight across an air hockey table
It keeps doing what it was doing
items.a: see items
items.why: Whenever motion starts, stops, speeds up, slows down or turns, a force is acting: a kick, friction, a hand. Things that stay still, or keep moving straight at a steady speed, need no force. A strong answer sorts the slowing cycle as a force, friction, and not as stopping by itself.

items.p: Meenakshi says, 'If you stop pushing a moving thing, it stops by itself.' Is she right?
items.why: False. A moving thing keeps moving until a force stops it. On Earth that force is usually friction or air resistance, which is why it seems to stop by itself. On ice it slides much further, and in space it would not stop at all.

items.p: Riya walks past a steel plate and lets go of rolled socks right above it. Where do they land?
opts: Past the plate, the way she was walking
items.why: The socks were moving forward with Riya, and they kept moving forward as they fell. So they landed past the plate. Picking 'on the plate' means thinking a dropped thing loses its forward motion as soon as you let go.

items.p: In the coin and card trick, explain why the coin drops into the tumbler when you flick the card fast. Use the word 'inertia'.
items.a: The coin is still, and because of inertia it stays still. The fast flick rubs it for only a moment, too short to move it. So the card goes and the coin stays, and gravity pulls it down into the tumbler.
items.why: A strong answer says the coin stays still because no force acted on it long enough, and that gravity then pulls it down.

items.p: Your helper watched the walking drop from the side. Draw the path of the rolled socks through the air, from your hand to the floor. Draw the plate too.
items.a: A curve that starts at the hand, goes forward and down, and lands past the plate.
items.why: Seen from the side, the socks move forward and fall at the same time, so the path curves. A strong drawing shows the socks landing past the plate, in the direction of walking.
items.art: A stick figure walking, with a plate on the floor ahead, and blank space for the path.

items.p: Arjun rolls a marble down the same ramp onto a towel, a doormat and bare tiles. On which does it roll furthest?
items.why: The bare tiles are the smoothest, so they give the least friction, and the marble rolls furthest. The towel's rough fibres give the most friction, so it stops soonest.

items.p: The grip between two surfaces that slows a rolling marble is called ____.
items.why: Friction is the grip between two surfaces that touch. It works against sliding and rolling, so it slows moving things down.

items.p: Farhan is standing in a bus that brakes suddenly. Which way does he lurch?
items.why: His body was moving forward with the bus, and it keeps moving forward when the bus slows. So he lurches forward. That is why standing passengers hold the bar.

items.p: A spacecraft far out in space, with its engines switched off, slows down and stops after a while.
items.why: False. In space there is almost no air and nothing to rub on, so there is almost no force to slow it. Voyager 1 has been coasting outwards for almost 50 years.

items.p: Why does a ball tossed straight up in a smooth train land back in your hand?
opts: It keeps moving forward with the train while it is in the air
Air inside the train pushes it
items.why: The ball was moving forward at the train's speed before you tossed it. In the air, nothing slows its forward motion, so it keeps up with you and lands in your hand.

items.p: Three of these happen because a moving thing keeps moving. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Coffee slops forward when a train brakes
A cyclist leans forward when the cycle hits a stone
Water keeps turning after the spoon is lifted out
A ball starts rolling when it is kicked
items.why: The kicked ball starts moving because a force, the kick, acts on it. The other three happen because something already moving kept moving when the things around it stopped.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the way a thing keeps doing what it is doing until a force changes it
the grip between surfaces that slows sliding and rolling
how much matter a thing has
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could also give an example of each, such as the coin on the card for inertia.

items.p: Two friends in Mysuru watch a cycle slow down and stop when the rider stops pedalling.

views.says: It stopped because nothing was pushing it any more. Moving things need a push to keep moving.
It stopped because friction and the air slowed it down. Without them, it would keep going.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you found in the marble rolling test. Then say what the other friend has noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Asha, using evidence: the marble rolled much further on smooth tiles than on a towel, so the slowing comes from friction, not from the missing push. It is fair to Pooja: in everyday life, things do stop when we stop pushing, so her idea fits what we usually see. Aristotle thought the same for nearly 2,000 years.
items.why: Both girls describe what they see. Only a test that changes the friction can show which explanation is right.

items.p: When a car brakes hard, why does a passenger without a seatbelt move forward?
items.a: Their body was moving forward with the car. When the car slows, nothing holds them, so their body keeps moving forward at the old speed until something stops it.
items.why: A strong answer says the body keeps its motion, and that the seatbelt gives the force that stops the passenger along with the car.

items.p: Put the steps of the walking drop in order.
items: Measure from the plate to where the socks landed
Put a plate in the middle of the floor
Walk past and let go when your hand is above the plate
Guess where the socks will land, and say why
a: Guess where the socks will land, and say why
Put a plate in the middle of the floor
Walk past and let go when your hand is above the plate
Measure from the plate to where the socks landed
items.why: First guess, so the test can surprise you. Then set up, drop, and measure.

items.p: Name one place in your home or on the road where you have seen inertia. Say what kept going, or what stayed still.
items.a: For example: when the auto braked, my school bag slid forward off the seat, because it kept moving.
items.why: A strong answer names a real moment and says what kept doing what it was doing.

items.p: In the walking drop, Kavya walked fast and the socks landed 70 cm past the plate. When she walked slowly, they landed 35 cm past. What does this show?
opts: Faster walking gives the socks more forward speed, so they go further while falling
Faster walking makes the socks heavier
The socks fall slower when you walk fast
items.why: The socks keep the speed they had in your hand. Walking faster gives them more forward speed, so they travel further forward in the same falling time.

items.p: Divya wants her walking-drop socks to land on the plate while she walks. When should she let go, and why?
items.a: Before her hand reaches the plate. The socks keep moving forward as they fall, so she must let go early for them to land on it.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that the socks keep their forward motion, and says to let go before the plate.

items.p: In the raw egg test, the finger stopped the shell, but the runny inside kept turning.
items.why: True. The finger touched only the shell. The inside kept moving because of inertia, and it set the shell turning again after the finger was lifted.

items.p: A boiled egg stays still after you stop it. A raw egg starts turning again. Explain the difference.
items.a: In a boiled egg, the inside is solid and fixed to the shell, so stopping the shell stops all of it. In a raw egg, the inside is runny, so it keeps turning when the shell stops, and it drags the shell round again.
items.why: A strong answer compares the solid and runny insides and uses the idea that moving things keep moving.

items.p: Lakshmi pulls the card slowly from under the coin on the tumbler. The coin moves with the card. Why is this different from a fast flick?
opts: With a slow pull, friction acts on the coin for longer, so it gets the coin moving
The coin is heavier when the card moves slowly
items.why: Friction between the card and the coin acts both times. With a slow pull, it acts for a long time and gets the coin moving with the card. With a fast flick, it acts for too short a time.

items.p: Which needs the longest distance to stop, if they are all going at the same speed?
items.why: The loaded lorry has the most mass, so it has the most inertia. Its brakes need longer to take away all that motion. This is why lorries keep a big gap on the highway.

items.p: Newton's first law says a thing stays at rest, or keeps moving at the same speed in a ____ line, unless a force acts on it.
items.why: Without a force, a moving thing goes straight. Turning, like slowing or speeding up, needs a force.

items.p: Sana swings a sock on a string in a circle and lets go. Which way does the sock fly?
opts: It keeps going round in a circle
Straight, the way it was moving at that moment
items.why: The string was the force turning the sock. Once she lets go, no force turns it, so it flies off straight, along the edge of the circle.

items.p: You cannot feel the Earth spinning, because it is not really moving.
items.why: False. The Earth does spin. In Chennai it carries you east at about 1,600 kilometres an hour. You can't feel it because the motion is smooth and steady, and everything around you moves with you, like in a smooth train.

items.p: Why does water slop forward in a tumbler when a bus brakes suddenly?
items.a: The water was moving forward with the bus. When the bus slows, the tumbler slows with it, but the water keeps moving forward for a moment, so it rises at the front.
items.why: A strong answer says the water keeps its motion while the tumbler slows down.

items.p: Arjun says, 'A marble on Earth always stops, so Newton's first law is wrong.' What would you tell him? Use your marble rolling results.
items.a: The law says a thing keeps moving unless a force acts. On Earth, friction and air resistance act on the marble. My results show that with less friction, on the tiles, it rolled much further than on the towel. So the law is right, and friction is the force that stops it.
items.why: A strong answer points to the pattern in the results: less friction, longer roll.

items.p: A stone slides a very long way on a frozen lake, but only a short way on a road. Explain why.
items.a: Ice is very smooth and slippery, so it gives very little friction. The road is rough and gives a lot of friction, which stops the stone quickly.
items.why: A strong answer names friction as the force that slows the stone, and compares how much each surface gives.

items.p: Two sisters in Hyderabad argue about the walking drop.

views.who: Nandini, aged 9, who dropped the socks
views.says: The socks fell straight down. I saw them fall right beside my leg.

views.who: Ritu, aged 7, who watched from the side
views.says: No, the socks fell in a curve. I saw them go forward as they fell.

items.ask: Who do you think is right? Explain what each sister saw, and why.
items.a: A strong answer says both describe truly what they saw. To Nandini, who was moving forward at the same speed, the socks stayed beside her leg, so they seemed to fall straight down. To Ritu, standing still, the socks moved forward and down at once, so they fell in a curve. The path you see depends on how you are moving.
items.why: This is a real puzzle in physics. How a thing moves always depends on what you compare it with.

items.p: Draw a view from above of a bus turning left. Show with an arrow which way a standing passenger leans.
items.a: A bus curving to the left, with an arrow on the passenger pointing to the right, towards the outside of the turn.
items.why: The passenger's body keeps going straight while the bus turns left, so they lean to the right, the outside of the turn.
items.art: An empty road curving to the left, seen from above.

items.p: A marble rolls down the same ramp onto four surfaces. Order them from the shortest roll to the longest.
items: Ice
A bath towel
Bare tiles
A doormat
items.why: The more friction a surface gives, the shorter the roll. The towel gives the most and ice the least.

items.p: Match each moment to what explains it.
pairs: The coin drops into the tumbler
The marble stops on the towel
The passenger leans out on a turn
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each moment shows one part of Newton's first law, or the force that changes motion.

items.p: You are sitting still on a sofa. The Earth spins, and it also carries you round the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second. Are you still or moving? Explain your answer.
items.a: Both, depending on what I compare with. Compared with the sofa and the room, I am still. Compared with the Sun, I am moving very fast. 'Still' always means still compared with something.
items.why: A strong answer sees that motion is always measured compared with something else, and gives both comparisons.

items.p: Three people talk about why a thrown cricket ball keeps moving after it leaves the bowler's hand.

views.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,300 years ago
views.says: The air rushes round behind the ball and keeps pushing it along.

views.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, in 1687
views.says: Nothing needs to push it. A moving thing keeps moving until a force changes it.
In my walking drop, nothing pushed the socks forward after I let go, and they still went forward.

items.ask: Which idea fits the evidence best? Use something you tested. Then say why Aristotle's idea seemed sensible in his time.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Newton and Kavya, with evidence: in space, with no air at all, Voyager 1 keeps moving, so air cannot be what keeps things going. The air actually slows a thrown ball down. Aristotle's idea seemed sensible because on Earth everything stops unless something keeps pushing, and nobody could test motion without air.
items.why: Aristotle's idea was believed for nearly 2,000 years. Tests with less and less friction, and travel in space, showed it was wrong.

items.p: Gassendi had stones dropped from the top of a ship's mast while the ship moved fast. Where did they land?
opts: At the foot of the mast
items.why: The stones were moving forward with the ship before they were dropped. They kept that motion as they fell, so they landed at the foot of the mast. This showed that the old argument against a moving Earth was wrong.

items.p: People once said, 'If the Earth were moving, a stone dropped from a tower would land far behind it.' Explain what is wrong with this argument.
items.a: The stone is moving with the Earth and the tower before it is dropped. While it falls, it keeps that motion, so it stays with the tower and lands at its foot, just as the socks kept moving with me.
items.why: A strong answer uses inertia and links it to the walking drop or Gassendi's ship.

items.p: A pilot flying a plane must drop a food parcel to people on an island. Should she let go before, above, or after the plane is over the island? Why?
items.a: Before. The parcel moves forward at the plane's speed and keeps moving forward as it falls. If she let go right above the island, it would land past it.
items.why: A strong answer applies the walking drop to a new case, and says why the parcel goes forward.

items.p: In the hover puck project, the puck glided about 3 metres and a plain CD slid about 10 cm from the same tap. What does this show about friction and inertia?
items.a: The puck rode on air, so there was almost no friction. With almost nothing to slow it, it kept moving much longer. This shows that moving things keep moving, and friction is what stops them.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers as evidence and names friction as the force that made the difference.

items.p: Which of these has the most inertia?
items.why: Inertia grows with mass. The full almirah has the most mass, so it is hardest to start, stop or turn.

items.p: Why does a raw egg wobble and spin slowly when you first twist it?
opts: Its runny inside stays still at first, while the shell turns
It is lighter than a boiled egg
items.why: When you twist the shell, the runny inside does not turn at once, because of inertia. It drags on the shell, so the raw egg is hard to spin fast and wobbles.

items.p: A girl tosses a ball straight up in a train that is slowing down for a station. Where will it land?
opts: A little ahead of her hand, towards the front of the train
A little behind her, towards the back of the train
items.why: The ball keeps the speed it had when tossed. The train and her hand slow down while it is in the air, so the ball gets ahead and lands a little in front.

items.p: Newton's law tells us what moving things do, but not why they have inertia. Do you think scientists will ever find out why? Give a reason.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: yes, because scientists have already found out where most mass comes from. Or: maybe not, because every answer leads to a new 'why'.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason and shows it understands that the law describes what happens without saying why.

items.p: A marble rolls along a perfectly smooth floor with no friction and no air at all. What happens?
opts: It slows down and stops after a while
It keeps rolling at the same speed for ever
items.why: With no force at all acting on it along the floor, nothing changes its motion. So it keeps going at the same speed in a straight line. This is Newton's first law.

items.p: Aryabhata compared a person in a moving boat, who sees the trees on the bank move backwards, to people on the turning Earth, who see the stars move west. Explain his idea in your own words.
items.a: In a moving boat, you feel still, and the trees seem to move the other way. In the same way, the Earth turns smoothly and we feel still, so the stars seem to move across the sky the other way, though it is really us who are moving.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the smooth motion is not felt, and that it makes still things seem to move the opposite way.

items.p: Design a safety feature for a school bus that would protect children if it braked suddenly. Draw it and label how it works.
items.a: Any sensible design, such as seatbelts, high padded seat backs, or soft bars in front of each seat, with labels saying how it stops children safely.
items.why: A strong design gives the children's bodies a force that stops them gently along with the bus, instead of letting them keep moving into something hard.
items.art: An empty outline of a bus seen from the side, with rows of seats.

items.p: A heavier coin in the card trick stays behind better than a light one, because it has more inertia.
items.why: True. More mass means more inertia, so the short rub from the flicked card moves a heavy coin even less. Stacked coins drop into the tumbler very reliably.

items.p: Sort these by what changed the motion: friction, gravity, or a push or pull from a person.
cats: A push or pull from a person
items: A marble stops on a towel
Friction
The coin falls into the tumbler
Gravity
A footballer kicks the ball
A push or pull from a person
A cycle slows when its brakes rub the wheel
Friction
A cricket ball curves down to the ground
Gravity
A fielder's hands stop the ball
A push or pull from a person
items.a: see items
items.why: Every change in motion has a force behind it. A strong answer names a force for each change and sees that brakes work by friction.

items.p: Three of these show a still thing staying still. Which is the odd one out?
opts: The coin stays put when the card is flicked
The top carrom coins drop when the bottom one is hit out
A leaf on water keeps pointing the same way when the bowl turns
A dough passenger flies off a toy car that crashes
items.why: The dough passenger was moving and kept moving. The other three were still and stayed still while something around them moved.

applications: Seatbelts and child car seats hold passengers when a car stops suddenly.
Helmets protect riders who are thrown forward off a two-wheeler.
Lorry and bus drivers keep a long gap on the highway, because a heavy vehicle needs a long distance to stop.
Spacecraft such as Voyager 1 and India's Mangalyaan coast through space for months with their engines off.
Planes dropping food parcels in floods let go well before they are above the target.
Shopkeepers tie down loads on bullock carts, tempos and cycles so they don't slide off when the vehicle stops.
Cricket fielders pull their hands back as they catch, so the ball is stopped more gently.
Washing machines spin water out of clothes: the drum turns, but the water flies off straight through the holes.

open_questions.q: Why do things have inertia at all?
open_questions.why_open: The law has passed every test, but nobody can say for certain why mass resists changes in motion. Mach's idea, that it comes from the rest of the universe, has not been shown to be true or false.

open_questions.q: Is there anywhere in the universe that is truly still?
open_questions.why_open: The Earth moves round the Sun, the Sun moves round the middle of our galaxy, and the galaxy moves too. Physics says there is no one place that counts as 'really still', but people still argue about what that means.

open_questions.q: Will Voyager 1 keep moving for ever?
open_questions.why_open: Space is almost empty, so very little slows it. In about 40,000 years it will pass a star called Gliese 445, still far from it. Nobody knows what it might meet in millions of years.

open_questions.q: Exactly where does the mass of an atom come from?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know most of it comes from energy deep inside the atom's centre, and they can calculate much of it. Some details are still being worked out.
