maths.problem: In the walking drop, Kavya's socks landed 30 cm, 40 cm and 35 cm past the plate when she walked slowly. Put the results in order. Which is the middle result?
maths.answer: 30 cm, 35 cm, 40 cm. The middle result is 35 cm.
maths.explain: In order from smallest to biggest: 30, 35, 40. The middle one is 35 cm. The middle result is a fair single number for the three tries, because it is not the biggest or the smallest.
maths.context: This is about the walking drop. You let go of rolled socks above a plate while walking, and measure how far past the plate they land.
maths.why_maths: Three tries never give exactly the same number. Ordering them and taking the middle one gives one fair result to compare.

maths.problem: Walking slowly, the socks landed about 35 cm past the plate. Walking fast, about 70 cm past. How many times as far is that? What does the pattern tell you?
maths.answer: 2 times as far. Walking about twice as fast sends the socks about twice as far.
maths.explain: 70 divided by 35 is 2. Check: 35 + 35 = 70. The faster you move, the further the socks go while they fall. That fits the idea that they keep the speed you gave them.
maths.context: This is about the walking drop. You walked slowly and then fast past a plate, and dropped rolled socks above it.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two numbers by division shows a pattern: twice the speed, twice the distance.

maths.problem: From the same ramp, the marble rolled 20 cm on a towel, 60 cm on a doormat and 240 cm on tiles. Draw a bar chart. How much further did it roll on tiles than on the towel?
maths.explain: 240 minus 20 is 220. So it rolled 220 cm further on the tiles. On the bar chart, the tiles bar is 12 times as tall as the towel bar, because 20 times 12 is 240.
maths.context: This is about the marble rolling test. You rolled a marble down a ruler ramp onto three floors and measured how far it went.

chart.title: How far the marble rolled from the same ramp

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which surface let the marble go furthest, and the subtraction says by how much.

maths.problem: The marble rolled 240 cm on tiles. A friend says, 'On ice, with even less friction, it might roll 10 times as far.' How far would that be, in metres?
maths.explain: 240 times 10 is 2,400 cm. There are 100 cm in a metre, so 2,400 cm is 24 metres. That is longer than most flats! It shows why things slide so far on ice.
maths.context: This is about the marble rolling test, and imagining an even more slippery floor made of ice.
maths.why_maths: Changing centimetres into metres helps us picture how far 2,400 cm really is.

maths.problem: In the raw egg test, egg B started turning again 3 times out of 3, egg D 3 times out of 3, and eggs A and C 0 times out of 3. Make a tally chart. Which eggs were raw?
maths.answer: B and D were raw. A and C were boiled.
maths.explain: A tally chart shows 3 marks for B, 3 for D, and none for A and C. A raw egg starts turning again because its runny inside keeps moving. So B and D were raw. Testing 3 times makes sure one lucky try did not fool us.
maths.context: This is about the egg test. You spin each egg, stop it with one finger and let go, to see if it starts turning again.
maths.why_maths: Tallying the tries shows a clear pattern, so we can decide from evidence, not from one try.

roots.context: We have learned that things keep doing what they are doing until a force changes it. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You let go of the socks right above the plate, yet they landed past it. While you carried them, they moved forward with you. After you let go, nothing pushed them forward, but they kept going. A moving thing carries its motion with it until a force takes it away.
deep_truth.habit: We split things into still and moving, and think still is natural while moving needs a cause. But the socks needed no push to keep moving. Only a change in motion needs a cause, a force.
deep_truth.evidence: In the walking drop, the socks landed about 35 cm past the plate at a slow walk and about 70 cm past at a fast walk. Standing still, they landed on it. Nothing pushed them forward after they left the hand.

three.who_am_i: Your body has inertia too. When a bus brakes, you keep moving forward until something stops you.
three.what_is_life: A cheetah or a running child must push on the ground to start and to stop, because their body keeps doing what it is doing.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth carries you, your home and the sea round the Sun very fast and very smoothly. You move together, so you feel still.

roots.thread: Before you let go, you and the socks moved as one. After you let go, the socks went on alone, still carrying the motion you had shared. The Earth does this for all of us. Every person, tree, river and building on the Earth shares the same motion round the Sun. Our separate journeys across a room or a city all happen inside that one shared movement.

teachings.teaching: A person in a moving boat sees the still trees on the bank moving backwards. In the same way, people on the turning Earth see the still stars moving west.
teachings.link: Aryabhata saw that a smooth motion you share cannot be felt, only seen in what is outside you. That is exactly the smooth train and the walking drop.

teachings.teaching: No one can stay even for a moment without acting.
teachings.link: Science finds the same for the body: even sitting still on the sofa, you are moving with the Earth all the time. Nothing on Earth is ever truly at rest.

teachings.teaching: When this is, that is. From the arising of this, that arises.
teachings.link: Newton's first law says the same about motion: no change happens without a cause. If a moving thing slows, turns or stops, a force made it happen.

science.text: Newton's first law: things stay at rest, or keep moving straight at a steady speed, unless a force acts. It has passed every test for over 300 years.
No experiment done inside a smoothly moving room can show whether the room is moving or still.
Why things have inertia at all has no agreed answer. Mach's idea, that it comes from the rest of the universe, is still argued about.

other_view.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, and the everyday feeling of most people
other_view.view: Rest is the natural state of things on Earth. A stone, a cart or a ball moves only while something moves it, and when that stops, it comes to rest. This fits almost everything we see around us every day.

practice.title: Feel the start and the stop
practice.say: Let's sit on the floor with our eyes closed. Take three slow breaths. Right now, the Earth is carrying us round the Sun, faster than any rocket. Can you feel it? Now let's stand up and walk slowly across the room. When I clap, stop at once. Did you feel your body lean forward? Let's walk again, and stop again. Now sit down, close your eyes, and take three more slow breaths. Which did you feel, the smooth moving or the stopping?
practice.kid: Sit on the floor. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. The Earth is carrying you fast. Can you feel it? Now walk slowly. Stop suddenly. Did your body lean? Sit and breathe three times. Which did you feel?

ask: In the walking drop, you saw the socks fall straight, and your helper saw a curve. Can two true views of the same thing be different?
If you cannot feel the Earth moving, what else might be moving that we cannot feel?
Is anything in the world ever truly still?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged on a terrace at night with eyes closed, the Earth drawn as a gentle curve beneath them with a faint arrow showing it moving, and stars above.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. The walking drop needs only rolled socks, a plate and about 4 metres of floor, so it works in a flat corridor or hall. Rolled socks or a rice bag are used because a ball bounces and rolls away. Falling from chest height takes under half a second, so at a slow walk the socks land roughly 20 to 50 cm past the plate and at a fast walk roughly 50 to 90 cm past, which is easy to see and measure. Children must walk, not run. The coin and card trick works best with a five- or ten-rupee coin and a flick straight sideways. The egg test needs boiled eggs fully cooled, a touch of only about one second, and gentle spins on a large plate. Families who do not use eggs use the water-turning activity, which shows the same idea. In the marble test, a marble on smooth tiles can roll to the wall, so the step says to lower the ramp and redo all three surfaces. The hover puck needs an old CD and an airtight seal, or it will not glide. The train toss is done seated, gently, with a grown-up, and only on smooth stretches. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.context: Can the Earth really be moving, when a dropped stone falls straight down? This card tells how people found out.
how_we_found_out.who: Aryabhata, an Indian astronomer, Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist, and Pierre Gassendi, a French priest and scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People argued that if the Earth were moving, a stone dropped from a tower would be left behind and land far from its foot. In the same way, they said a stone dropped from the mast of a moving ship would land behind the mast.
how_we_found_out.story: Around 499 CE, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote that the Earth turns. He said the stars only seem to move west, the way trees on a river bank seem to move backwards to someone in a moving boat. For more than a thousand years, most people elsewhere disagreed. In Europe, they had a strong argument. If the Earth were moving, a stone dropped from a tall tower would be left behind, and land far from the tower's foot. It lands right at the foot. So, they said, the Earth must be still. They added that a stone dropped from the top of a moving ship's mast lands behind the mast. In 1632, Galileo Galilei answered that the stone moves forward with the ship, and keeps moving forward as it falls. But had anyone really tried it? In 1640, the French priest and scientist Pierre Gassendi did. On a galley, a ship rowed by many oars, moving fast in the sea off Marseille, stones were dropped from the top of the mast. They landed at the foot of the mast, not behind it. A moving stone keeps its motion, so the old argument against a moving Earth was wrong.
